title: Hands-on: Three Operator Cases
points: Run one notebook to understand three operator studies.
90 minutes / three short exercises / no coding experience required
source_label: Setup: COLAB_GUIDE.md; Classroom_Labs.ipynb.
note: Open the one required Classroom Labs notebook. This hands-on workshop uses 80 slides and 180 teaching minutes, with breaks outside that total. Start with a twelve-minute Stanford concept block: show each original source figure, then its simple grid adaptation. The next seven minutes prepare Colab and run L0–L1. Learners calculate fresh numerical results and inspect separately labeled saved Llama replies. No default cell calls an LLM or operates equipment. Keep the notebook in order and run L10B only after L10. Work in pairs and use the six-page participant guide. Presenter affiliations were supplied by the presenters. The IEEE ComSoc theme is an independent educational adaptation.

title: What is agentic AI?
points: An LLM agent works toward a goal by choosing tools, reading their results and choosing what to do next.
note: Use the architectural definition in Anthropic, Building effective agents: an agent lets the LLM direct its process and tool use. Agentic AI is a broad term; here it means a system organized around this bounded loop. An AI agent is the component that chooses and follows steps. A tool is a permitted software function that returns a result. Point to the goal, model choice, executable tool, returned evidence and feedback arrow. The application stores case facts and prior results as the context supplied at the next model request. If a required check is missing, the outcome remains HOLD. Stop or return a proposal only under the fixed workflow rules. Do not imply that feedback alone establishes agency: conventional programs can also branch and loop. Our default notebook calculates engineering results now but replays the actual old Llama choices. No live model service is needed. Stanford source: Monica Lam, CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction, Fall 2026, p.2 describes function calling and agentic workflows. The goal-and-feedback drawing is our grid teaching adaptation, supported by the separate bounded-agent architecture citation. This is not an original Stanford power-system diagram.
caption: Grid teaching adaptation of the Stanford lecture, p.2. Model choices are recorded; calculations can run now.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.2.

title: Stanford: tool calls become a workflow
points: A tool call runs one step. An agentic workflow links steps and uses their results to continue or stop.
note: Show the two original capability panels from Monica Lam’s Stanford CS224V introduction, p.2. The left panel introduces model-selected function calling. The right panel describes multi-step planning, tool use and self-correction. Our plain-language sentence connects the panels to the preceding bounded-loop teaching drawing. The following source-and-lab pairs show why tool results, explicit goals and checked evidence matter in each case. In that example Llama requests a named action and Python validates the JSON choice before calling an existing function; it does not use a native tool_calls protocol. Conventional software can also loop, and a chatbot may itself contain an agent. Here we identify the agentic feature by the model’s permitted next-step choice based on returned evidence. The class replays those old model choices while numerical cells calculate current results. Source lecture figure is shown unchanged within the documented crop.
caption: Original Stanford lecture excerpt, p.2. Next, connect tool use to evidence, task rules and decision checks.

title: Stanford example: tools need clear rules
points: Write down the required inputs, permitted tools, limits and stop rules.
Our lab keeps those rules in Python. A language reply cannot change the limits.
note: Stanford connection: Lam p.40 and the published Genie Worksheets paper emphasize developer-defined workflows and knowledge sources. The published framework uses an algorithmic runtime to enforce a supplied policy, with LLMs used for language understanding and response generation. Our lab uses custom Python functions, not Genie Worksheets. The application analogy is to specify the task and prevent a language reply from silently changing its limits or filling missing required inputs. A passed calculation does not prove that the task description was correct. The figure shown here is an actual excerpt from the supplied Stanford lecture. Ask the audience to point to the claim-checking or policy step, then identify the corresponding Python check in our lab. We borrow the design habit; the notebook does not run WikiChat or Genie. Their non-grid benchmarks are not electrical performance results.
caption: Original Stanford lecture excerpt, p.40. The lab adopts the idea of explicit rules in Python.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.40.

title: Restoration: the service goal shapes the plan
points: An agent must keep the stated service goal. L6 lets you see how that goal changes the plan.
caption: Our grid adaptation of explicit task rules. L6 uses the same 40 kW varied tie and 100 kW fixed tie for both goals.
note: The preceding Genie excerpt motivates writing down the task and its rules before calling a function. In L6 the goal is part of the optimization problem: priority weighting serves 130 total kW, including 90 critical kW; maximizing total service gives 140 total kW, including 30 critical kW. The 40 kW limit belongs to one varied tie, while another tie stays fixed at 100 kW. Totals also include the 40 kW load at node 1 upstream of those ties. A 40 kW varied-tie limit is not a cap on total system service. Each stacked bar uses the same scale. Critical service is cyan; other service is blue. Ask which goal better matches an illustrative request to prioritize a hospital. The numerical model uses abstract critical loads, not an actual hospital dataset. Later learners run both goals and change the tie capacity. L6 is a direct Python calculation, not a live LLM agent. An agent coordinating such a study must preserve the requested goal and explain the returned tradeoff. The separate L10B feeder-catalog archive supplies actual saved Llama choices; it differs from this six-node L6 model. Our notebook does not implement Genie Worksheets.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.40; Classroom Labs L6.

title: Stanford: language and decision checks
points: The lecture turns written facts into constraints, then uses a solver to check a decision.
Our grid adaptation: Llama requests a study, Python checks its results, and the operator reviews the proposal.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.53.
note: This original diagram selection comes from the function row on p.53 of Monica Lam’s introduction. It shows a clinical-trial example, not a power-system experiment. The language model translates written facts into an SMT representation; a separate solver derives a decision from those constraints. SMT means satisfiability modulo theories, a way to express and solve logical constraints. MaxSAT supports the lecture’s search for conditions that change a decision. The lecture also states that the formalization may not be completely faithful, so correctness remains relative to the represented constraints. Our application is an analogy: Llama requests the permitted estimate or control tool and Python checks numerical limits. An operator must still confirm the trust assumption and review the proposed action. Our notebook does not run an SMT/MaxSAT solver or prove formal electrical safety. Preview the HOLD/PROPOSE distinction now; participants will calculate the L9 outcomes later with their stated model and trusted-data assumption.
eyebrow: Stanford source example / grid teaching analogy
image_credit: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.53.
image_transformation: Unchanged vector selection from the presenter-supplied Stanford lecture, p.53; Poppler PNG rendering. Exact crop and source/image hashes: research/stanford_sources/excerpt_manifest.json.
caption: Clinical-trial research example. SMT represents logical constraints; MaxSAT helps find decision-changing conditions.

title: Cyber: a clear answer still needs evidence
points: L8 tests whether readings can look consistent but be wrong. L9 adds a trust assumption and recovery checks.
caption: Our grid adaptation of separating language from checks. The fixed L9 example returns HOLD or PROPOSE under stated assumptions.
note: Relate the original Stanford clinical example to this lab without importing a formal guarantee. L8 fits readings to a four-bus DC model using WLS, weighted least squares. Its small residual is a measure of fit, not proof of sensor truth; the known simulation truth is used only for teaching error comparisons. L9 is a separate fixed recovery fixture. Without trusted replacement data it returns HOLD. With three additional readings assumed trusted and a successful modeled recovery check, it returns PROPOSE. The yes branch depicts this fixed example with passing numerical checks; a real study also needs every required check to pass. The calculation does not authenticate the extra readings. Later learners run L8, vary the attack scale, then reset before the independent L9 example. Python performs these calculations now. A coordinating agent should request evidence and retain HOLD when a required premise is missing; saved L10B replies show a separate recorded cyber case. Our code uses numerical checks, not the Stanford SMT/MaxSAT runtime.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.53; Classroom Labs L8–L9.

title: Ask four questions about a study result
points: Find the tool result, assumptions, rules and the operator’s next step.
If a claim has no supporting result, leave it unresolved and request the missing check.
note: Lam’s pp.52–53 distinguish verifiable rationale, explicit assumptions, policy consistency and actionable next conditions. Translate these into four plain questions: which tool supports this claim, which inputs and model were used, were the same limits and service priorities kept, and what must the operator review next? Our power-flow, optimization and evidence-binding checks are numerical/software checks. They do not inherit the lecture’s SMT correctness claims. Ask pairs to apply the questions to one L10B explanation and to the full-scope HOLD at L12. We show only the actual public returned reasons, not hidden chain-of-thought. This closes the twelve-minute opening concept block. Point out that all three labs will use these questions; participants do not need to memorize a framework or run ahead.
caption: Grid teaching adaptation of Monica Lam’s accountability concepts, Stanford CS224V introduction, pp.52–53.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, pp.52–53.

title: Run L1: does the evidence still match?
points: Read binding_pass: does the record match the same inputs and command?
Expect True, False, False. Changing the load or command breaks that match.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L0–L1; cells classroom-002 and classroom-004.
note: Evidence binding means matching a checked record to the exact inputs, proposed command and returned result, using content hashes. Treat L1 as a same-content check, not a test that a physical action passes its limits. The first row keeps the request and command unchanged. The next two rows change a request field or command field, so binding_pass is True, False, False. A failed match calls for new evidence; it does not prove the changed action fails its limits. A matching hash also does not authenticate a sensor.
caption: Reference L1 output: only the unchanged request and command match the evidence.

title: Voltage: open L2
points: MPC makes a forecast-based plan. SAC is a saved learned controller.
Check limits first. Then compare penalty score J; smaller is preferred after the checks pass.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: The feeder is a synthetic SMART-DS Greensboro-area example, not a measured utility circuit. The command sets active- and reactive-power participation for an inverter fleet. MPC, model predictive control, uses a system model and a short forecast to calculate a plan under limits; here the proposed command is the first step of that plan. SAC, Soft Actor–Critic, is a saved controller learned from rewards. It produces a proposal from old weights without training again. The default calculation covers medium-voltage (MV) phases and MV line currents, with simplified low-voltage (LV) aggregation. Feasible means the proposal passes the limits represented by that model. Compare the penalty score J only after checking those limits; smaller J is preferred for this stated objective. Run L0 and L1 first.
caption: Synthetic SMART-DS teaching feeder; not an operating utility circuit.

title: MPC plans; SAC proposes
points: Both tools propose control settings. The same numerical check tests their voltage and current limits.
note: MPC uses a model and a short forecast to optimize a plan; this lab applies its first action. SAC is a saved policy learned through reinforcement learning; it produces a new control proposal using old weights, without training again. Neither is the coordinating LLM. The outer agent can choose which permitted study to request. L2 calls both tools directly and displays their checks; this cell alone is not a live LLM agent. Later recorded P3 figures illustrate Llama coordinating the existing tools. Define per unit when the control-limit slide introduces the voltage scale: 1.0 p.u. is the stated base value. Explain MILP and WLS only in their respective cases.
caption: MPC: model predictive control. SAC: Soft Actor–Critic. These are control tools inside the larger workflow.

title: A real agent changes its next step
points: The failed tool result leads to a fallback check. Passing the checks still leaves human review.
note: This is an actual saved Llama 3.1:8b voltage episode, not a fabricated interactive exchange. Call 1 selects VERIFY_SAC_FIRST; the numerical check returns 111.966607 percent of allowed current and two current violations. Call 2 selects USE_MPC_PLAN; its numerical check returns 99.604410 percent of allowed current and no recorded violations. The SAC and MPC tools already exist; Llama does not invent or solve the power flow. The arrows show tool-request, result, next-request, result. Call 3 selects REVIEW_EVIDENCE. Human acknowledgment remains PENDING and equipment_dispatch is False. This separate P3 MV/LV OpenDSS archive differs from the fresh L2 exercise and from L3 test_01. Later voltage slides display the exact public returned reasons; learners can replay the source in L10B after completing the three cases. The fixed comparator reaches the same numerical outcome, so the trace illustrates coordination rather than a proven performance improvement. This recorded example now follows the MPC/SAC definition slide in the voltage case, after Colab setup. It remains a preview; run the complete episode in L10B later.
caption: Recorded P3 example, separate from L2. 111.966607% and 99.604410% are rounded here.
eyebrow: Recorded P3 example / separate from the L2 calculation

title: Control settings and limits
points: a sets active-power participation; b sets reactive-power participation.
Check the inverter limits, modeled voltages and allowed line current.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: Active power delivers net energy; reactive power supports the AC voltage and current balance. The command uses P_i = a S_i and Q_i = b S_i. Its bounds are 0 <= a <= 1, |b| <= 0.44 and a^2 + b^2 <= 1. Modeled voltages must be between 0.95 and 1.05 per unit (p.u.), where values are divided by a stated base. RATING_FRACTION=0.80 sets allowed current to 80% of the nominal rating. The displayed current percentage uses this reduced allowance as its denominator. Passing the inverter bounds alone does not show that network limits pass.
caption: Active and reactive settings share the inverter’s power limit.

title: A tool is a Python function in this lab
points: A tool takes defined inputs and returns evidence. The notebook lets you see both.
note: Find the actual function call on the next slide. The first two cell lines set the load scale and current allowance; the helper returns numerical proposals, checks and a table for plotting. A tool can be an optimizer, simulator, estimator, lookup or evidence checker. It is not the LLM itself. The student initiates this direct function call with the play button. In the separate recorded workflow Llama selects a named action, the Python application validates that action and its inputs, then invokes a permitted numerical function. Do not claim that the L2 helper uses a live agent gateway. Saving a notebook is separate from keeping a runtime: after a reset, rerun setup and earlier cells.
caption: L2 calls lab.voltage_lab(LOAD_SCALE, RATING_FRACTION) directly. Recorded agent coordination is separate.

title: Run L2 with the default inputs
points: Run all of L2 to calculate the MPC plan and check the saved SAC controller’s proposal.
Read feasible, current_step_J and max_allowed_current_pct.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: Start with LOAD_SCALE=1.0 and RATING_FRACTION=0.80. The saved SAC actor produces a new proposal by inference; it is not trained in this cell. Both proposals pass the default classroom checks. MPC has the lower current-step J for this case and objective. This single result does not establish a universal control advantage. The output field feasible reports whether the modeled limits pass; current_step_J is this step’s penalty score, and max_allowed_current_pct is maximum current as a percentage of the reduced allowance.

title: Read the voltage and current plots
points: Left: compare the sorted modeled voltages with the allowed band.
Right: compare line current with the 100% allowed-current limit.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: The left panel sorts each voltage curve separately. The same horizontal position means the same rank, not necessarily the same physical bus. The right panel reports current relative to the reduced allowance. Use the output table for exact extrema and feasibility; do not decide acceptance from a plot alone.
caption: Reference L2 plots; rerun L2 to calculate plots for your inputs.

title: Check limits before comparing scores
points: Default MPC passes: current use 73.62%, penalty score J about 0.03110.
Default saved SAC passes: current use 51.68%, J about 0.43643.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: In the reference execution, MPC returns a=0.960307 and b=-0.111114, with Vmin=1.023874 and Vmax=1.038709 p.u. SAC returns a=0.340066 and b=0.014024, with Vmin=1.013243 and Vmax=1.030000 p.u. Values may vary slightly with the solver or dependency version. Lower current use need not mean lower J, because the objective also includes service and control terms. Check feasibility before comparing J. Both voltage extrema are within the stated 0.95–1.05 p.u. band for this represented MV model.
caption: Reference L2 output with LOAD_SCALE=1.0 and RATING_FRACTION=0.80.

title: A rule and a tool result answer different questions
points: A document can tell us the limit. A numerical tool tells us how the proposal compares with it.
Keep the source, the measured or calculated value, and the remaining checks together.
note: Stanford connection: the lecture’s WikiChat discussion, pp.17–25, separates finding material from checking factual claims. Apply the habit to a grid study: retrieving a current limit is different from calculating current for a candidate. The displayed 99.604410% value belongs to the separate archived P3 OpenDSS replay, not to the learner’s fresh L2 result. This example supports only that current check under its recorded model. A sentence, retrieved document or citation does not establish full-network feasibility. Treat the input limits as the task policy. A text source describes the rule; the solver evaluates the particular proposal.
caption: Teaching analogy. The number shown comes from the recorded P3 replay, which is separate from L2.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, pp.17–25; recorded P3 current check.

title: What runs now and what was recorded
points: The current cell calculates new results. The saved Llama reply keeps its original inputs.
Changing your lab input does not rewrite the recorded agent study.
note: Point to these evidence modes throughout the session. Default classroom cells calculate fresh results without a live language-model call. L10B displays verified historical Llama choices, original reasons and associated recorded results. Changing your L2 or L6 input does not change those old replies. The final control-room diagrams are a proposed teaching design, not evidence of a deployed utility platform. No new equipment operation occurs in any of these modes. FRESH means calculated during the current execution. SAVED POLICY means old weights used for new inference. ARCHIVED ACTUAL LLM means an old reply with its original inputs and timing. This slide comes just before L3 so the distinction is applied immediately.

title: Run L5: check what the model covers

Start with tie capacities of 40, 60, 80, 100 and 120 kW. The solver enforces active-power balance, capacity limits, connection to a source, no loops in the energized graph, and exclusion of the faulted branch. An independent exhaustive search checks the priority score on this small graph. Agreement supports this formulation; it does not check the AC physics left out of the model.

title: Cyber: open L8
points: Use the separate four-bus DC model and its supplied readings.
Compare a residual alarm, which checks fit, with error against the known teaching truth.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L8; cell classroom-023; four-bus DC fixture.
note: The separate four-bus linear DC model has three unknown voltage angles, measured relative to a reference bus, and eight readings. This DC approximation is not a full AC estimator, malware detector or sensor-authentication system. Synthetic truth is known for the offline classroom comparison only. A residual checks how well the estimate fits the supplied readings; state error checks how far the estimate is from the known teaching truth.
caption: Four-bus linear DC teaching model; known synthetic truth is used only for offline comparison.

title: Best fit and true state are different
points: WLS finds the best fit to readings, giving more weight to lower stated uncertainty.
Residual J measures fit mismatch. State error uses teaching truth unavailable to an operator.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L8; cell classroom-023; four-bus DC fixture.
note: WLS means weighted least squares: find the state that best fits the readings, giving more influence to readings with smaller stated uncertainty. That weighting does not authenticate a reading. Here J is the residual mismatch statistic, not the voltage case’s penalty score. Its chi-square alarm threshold is about 15.086272 for five residual degrees of freedom at a 1% significance level. This calibration depends on the stated linear model and noise assumptions. An operator does not have the synthetic truth used to calculate the plotted state error. A small J does not establish that the readings are authentic.
caption: A good fit to readings does not show that those readings are authentic.

title: Run L8: compare two data attacks

source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L8; cell classroom-023; four-bus DC fixture.

This counterexample assumes knowledge of the linear measurement matrix H and access to the modeled unprotected channels. It is a declared defensive teaching model, not evidence of an incident at a utility.

title: Llama chooses; tools calculate; people decide
points: The agent coordinates a study. Numerical tools supply the checks. The operator reviews the proposal.
note: Use the three symbols to assign responsibilities: the speech box is Llama making a permitted choice and returning a public reason; the function is Python and OpenDSS calculating physical results and enforcing workflow limits; the person is the operator reviewing evidence and retaining operating authority. The Llama wrappers use constrained JSON interpreted by the application, rather than native tool_calls. Language explanations are not proof of physical correctness. In our replay the model may say REVIEW but the human acknowledgment is still PENDING. For each exercise work in pairs: one person runs while the other checks, then swap. Save the input, result, check and next decision. Stanford p.53 separates language understanding from checking a formal decision model in a clinical-trial example. The lab adaptation separates Llama coordination from Python numerical checks and operator review. This lab does not run SMT or MaxSAT, and the analogy supplies no formal guarantee about the grid model. This role reminder now introduces the closing advisory-pilot discussion, after the L12 readback.

title: Start a control-room pilot with a clear study request
points: Use an approved copy of the network data with a time stamp, topology version and limits.
If required data are missing or too old, return HOLD and name the missing information.
note: Proposed advisory pilot, not a deployment claim. F12 is an illustrative teaching feeder name. Read the study request aloud: compare the allowed voltage-support options, keep the stated current and voltage limits, show the worst margins and missing checks, and return a recommendation for review. The data owner defines acceptable age, source and quality rules. L1 and L7 illustrate matching inputs to results, but hashes alone do not authenticate those sources.

title: Give the assistant a small, controlled tool list
points: An approved interface supplies read-only data and study tools. Log every request and result.
Keep equipment commands in the utility’s separate authorized operating process.
note: Proposed advisory pilot. Walk through the lanes: operator, assistant, application-controlled tool gateway and engineering tools. Llama requests one permitted function; the application checks the request and executes the tool. A snapshot identifier binds the result to the input. The workshop Python functions are teaching counterparts, not SCADA adapters. NIST OT guidance supports controlled information flows, least privilege and logging. The exact pilot architecture is our teaching recommendation, not a NIST-certified design.
caption: Proposed advisory pilot — teaching design. Classroom functions are not live control-room interfaces.
source_label: Teaching proposal informed by NIST OT guidance and the cited notebook checks.

title: Check three things before returning a proposal
points: Check that the inputs match, the required limits pass and the required network parts were modeled.
Example: an MV-only PASS stays on HOLD when the request requires the full MV/LV network.
note: Proposed advisory pilot. Current data and a matching evidence packet are the first gate. The second gate checks stated engineering limits with approved tools. The third asks whether the calculations cover the request, including excluded low-voltage parts or required protection and dynamic studies. This is not a universal complete security checklist. It illustrates why L12 can produce a passing local calculation and still HOLD a broader request. Make missing evidence visible instead of allowing fluent text to fill the gap.
caption: Proposed advisory pilot — teaching design. A PASS is limited to its tested model and inputs.
source_label: Teaching proposal informed by NIST OT guidance and the cited notebook checks.

title: Give the operator a short evidence packet
points: Show the input snapshot, selected option, worst margins, rejected trials and missing checks.
The reviewer can ask for another study, reject the proposal or accept it for the next review step.
note: Proposed advisory pilot. Use three review questions: Does this match the current equipment, inputs and model? Did the required checks pass, with missing checks clear? What exactly am I approving, who owns the next step, and where is the record? Record the reviewer, reason, case snapshot and tool versions. Accepting a study result does not itself issue an equipment command. Authorized operating procedures and roles determine any later physical action. L12 practices only a simulated ID-bound readback.
caption: Proposed advisory pilot — teaching design. Review of a study is distinct from operating equipment.
source_label: Teaching proposal informed by NIST OT guidance and the cited notebook checks.

title: Adopt it in stages and measure the benefit
points: Begin with past cases, then read-only shadow work, then a limited pilot with named reviewers.
Compare against the same tools in a fixed script: correct studies, missed checks, time and rework.
note: Proposed advisory pilot. Historical replay lets engineers define expected outcomes and failure cases. Shadow use compares recommendations alongside the existing process without relying on them for equipment control. A limited pilot needs a named owner, training, an agreed scope and a way to stop use. Measure end-to-end elapsed time including review, correct completed studies, missed or stale inputs, overlooked limits and reviewer changes. Compare the same engineering tools with and without Llama. Our paired records show identical final numerical results, so there is no basis yet to promise higher accuracy, less operator workload or faster decisions. NIST AI RMF supports human roles, evaluation under realistic conditions and deactivation; these particular pilot metrics are our recommendation.
caption: Proposed advisory pilot — teaching design. Benefits must be measured against an appropriate baseline.
source_label: Teaching proposal informed by NIST OT guidance and the cited notebook checks.
